title: ABG and VBG
subtitle: Acid–base status, ventilation, oxygenation and lactate
summary: Acid–base status, ventilation, oxygenation and lactate
introduction: Use the analyser and local laboratory ranges. A VBG can support assessment of pH, bicarbonate and trends in carbon dioxide, but venous pO₂ must not be used to assess oxygenation. Record the oxygen device and flow or FiO₂ at the time of sampling.

rows.name: pH
notes: VBG pH is normally slightly lower than arterial pH.

rows.name: pCO₂
lowInterpretation: Supports respiratory alkalosis or respiratory compensation when interpreted with pH and bicarbonate.
highInterpretation: Supports respiratory acidosis or respiratory compensation when interpreted with pH and bicarbonate.
notes: PvCO₂ is normally slightly higher than arterial pCO₂.

rows.name: Bicarbonate
lowInterpretation: Supports metabolic acidosis or renal compensation for respiratory alkalosis.
highInterpretation: Supports metabolic alkalosis or renal compensation for respiratory acidosis.

rows.name: Base excess
lowInterpretation: A negative value supports a metabolic acid load.
highInterpretation: A positive value supports metabolic alkalosis or chronic compensation.

rows.name: pO₂
rows.referenceRange: Interpret with age, inspired oxygen and clinical context
lowInterpretation: PaO₂ below 8.0 kPa suggests hypoxaemic respiratory failure; confirm inspired oxygen and SpO₂.
notes: Do not use venous pO₂ to assess arterial oxygenation.

rows.name: Lactate
highInterpretation: 2.0–3.9 mmol/L is abnormal; at least 4.0 mmol/L is a major abnormality requiring urgent assessment of the cause.
notes: A normal lactate does not exclude sepsis, shock or another serious illness.

rows.name: Respiratory acidosis
notes: Consider hypoventilation, COPD/asthma fatigue, sedative/opioid effect, neuromuscular weakness or severe obesity hypoventilation. Raised bicarbonate may indicate chronic compensation or acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis.

rows.name: Metabolic acidosis
notes: Consider lactate, ketones, renal failure, diarrhoea, toxins and the anion gap. Low pCO₂ may indicate respiratory compensation.

rows.name: Mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis
rows.referenceRange: Low pH with raised pCO₂ and low bicarbonate

rows.name: Respiratory alkalosis
notes: Consider pain/anxiety only after excluding hypoxia, PE, sepsis, pregnancy, liver disease and salicylates.

rows.name: Metabolic alkalosis
notes: Consider vomiting, gastric losses, diuretics, hypokalaemia, mineralocorticoid excess or alkali administration.

rows.name: Mixed respiratory and metabolic alkalosis
rows.referenceRange: High pH with low pCO₂ and raised bicarbonate
notes: Both low pCO₂ and raised bicarbonate are driving the pH up.

calculations.title: Basic acid–base pattern
calculations.formula: rule-based interpretation of pH, pCO2 and bicarbonate
interpretation: This is a basic pattern recognition aid and does not calculate expected compensation.
Review base excess, anion gap, sample quality and the clinical picture; consider mixed disorders.

inputs.label: pH
inputs.validationMessage: Enter a plausible blood pH between 6.0 and 8.0.

urgentFindings: pH below 7.25 or a falling pH.
pH below 7.35 with raised pCO₂ and drowsiness or exhaustion.
PaO₂ below the expected range despite oxygen.
overrides: Escalate based on the patient and trajectory rather than a single threshold.
Always review potassium, glucose, ketones, lactate, haemoglobin and carboxyhaemoglobin/methemoglobin when clinically relevant.
